events.title: Amazon Founded
events.blurb: A former hedge-fund vice-president who had driven across the country from New York to Seattle with his wife, writing a business plan on the way, incorporated an online book retailer in the garage of a rented house in a Seattle suburb. He had chosen books because no single physical store could stock every book in print, but one big warehouse could. The company's first website was clunky; the logic was unstoppable.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1994 — Jeff Bezos. The company was originally called Cadabra; Bezos changed it after a lawyer misheard it as "cadaver." He considered and rejected relentless.com (now redirecting to Amazon).

events.title: Netscape IPO
events.blurb: A 16-month-old Silicon Valley company that had distributed free web browsers and had never turned a profit went public at $28 a share, opened at $71, and closed its first trading day at $58.25. Its 24-year-old co-founder was suddenly worth $58 million on paper. Wall Street had discovered the internet, and the next five years of stock-market mania had a starting gun.
events.revealBlurb: August 9, 1995 — Netscape Communications. Co-founder Marc Andreessen ended up on the cover of Time two years later with the caption "The Kid Who Tamed the Web." Microsoft's bundled Internet Explorer would eventually kill Netscape; the company sold to AOL in 1999.

events.title: Y2K Rollover
events.blurb: As the world's time zones successively crossed the boundary between the 20th and 21st centuries, decades of doomsday predictions — that computer systems storing years as two digits would interpret "00" as 1900 and crash vital infrastructure — largely failed to materialize. An estimated $300 billion had been spent worldwide on remediation code. Whether the peaceful transition vindicated the expense or exposed it as overblown remains contested.
events.revealBlurb: January 1, 2000 — New Zealand and Pacific islands hit midnight first, without incident. Actual bugs did occur — a French meteorological satellite briefly misreported dates, some slot machines froze, a few nuclear plants had cooling-monitor glitches — but nothing catastrophic. The fix, written in COBOL in the 1990s, may be the largest software project ever.

events.title: Instagram Launched
events.blurb: A two-person startup released a free iOS app that let users take photos, apply one of eleven retro filters, and share them to a simple timeline-based social network. It acquired 25,000 users on launch day and its first million within three months. Facebook bought the company for $1 billion in cash and stock eighteen months later, when it had thirteen employees and zero revenue.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 2010 — Kevin Systrom and Mike Krieger. Originally built as a location-based check-in app called Burbn. The $1 billion Facebook acquisition in April 2012 is now considered one of the great bargains in tech history.

events.title: Snapchat Launched
events.blurb: Three Stanford undergraduates released an iOS app that let users send photos that automatically disappeared a few seconds after being viewed. One founder had pitched the idea for a product-design class the previous spring and been told it was terrible. The app would grow explosively as a teenage-first social platform and introduce "Stories," a format quickly copied by every major competitor.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 2011 — Evan Spiegel, Bobby Murphy, and Reggie Brown. Originally named Picaboo. Facebook offered to acquire Snap for $3 billion in 2013; Spiegel said no. Snap went public in 2017 at a $24 billion valuation.

events.title: Truman Doctrine
events.blurb: Addressing a joint session of Congress, a U.S. president requested $400 million in aid for Greece and Turkey and announced a sweeping new foreign policy: the United States would support "free peoples" resisting armed minorities or outside pressures. The speech committed America to global containment of communism.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1947 — Harry Truman needed just 18 minutes. Behind the rhetoric: Britain, bankrupted by war, had quietly told Washington it could no longer prop up the Greek government. America stepped into the imperial vacuum.

events.title: People's Republic of China Proclaimed
events.blurb: Standing above a vast plaza in the Chinese capital, a revolutionary leader announced the founding of a new communist state after two decades of civil war and foreign occupation. His defeated nationalist rival retreated to an island 160 kilometres off the mainland coast and established a rival regime that persists today.
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1949 — Mao Zedong declared the PRC from the Tiananmen gate. Chiang Kai-shek fled to Taiwan with 2 million refugees and most of the mainland's gold reserves. The split still defines East Asian geopolitics.

events.title: Warsaw Pact Founded
events.blurb: Eight communist-bloc nations signed a mutual defense treaty in the Polish capital, creating a military alliance explicitly framed as a response to West Germany's admission into the rival Atlantic alliance ten days earlier. In practice, it institutionalized Soviet command over the armed forces of its eastern European satellites.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1955 — members included the USSR, Poland, East Germany, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania, Bulgaria, and Albania. It was dissolved in July 1991, six months before the USSR itself vanished. Most of its former members are now in NATO.

events.title: Moscow-Washington Hotline
events.blurb: Shaken by how close they had come to nuclear war the previous October, the United States and Soviet Union signed a memorandum of understanding establishing a direct teleprinter link between their capitals. Contrary to Hollywood, it was never a red telephone — it was a clunky, secure teletype system. The first test message read: "THE QUICK BROWN FOX JUMPS OVER THE LAZY DOG."
events.revealBlurb: June 20, 1963 — signed in Geneva. The line was first used in earnest in 1967 during the Arab-Israeli War. Today it's a secure email system; neither side actually picks up a red phone.

events.title: German Reunification
events.blurb: On a crisp autumn evening, a huge black, red, and gold flag was raised in front of the Reichstag building as the East German state ceased to exist and its 16 million citizens became part of the unified federal republic. Forty-five years of partition, imposed by four occupying armies, ended at the stroke of midnight. Crowds sang the national anthem for the first time as one country.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1990 — the date is now German Unity Day. The integration cost West Germany over €2 trillion over three decades. Many eastern cities still empty out; many western taxpayers still grumble about the "solidarity surcharge."

events.title: Compact Disc Launches
events.blurb: Sony and Philips released the Compact Disc — a 12-cm polycarbonate-and-aluminum disc encoding digital audio that could be read by a laser — along with the first commercially available CD players. The digital format eventually killed off the vinyl LP and the cassette, promising perfect sound quality and indestructibility (neither claim quite held up). The first commercial CD, launched in Japan, was Billy Joel's "52nd Street."
events.revealBlurb: October 1, 1982 — Sony, Philips launch the Compact Disc in Japan. European/US launch March 1983. The 74-minute maximum runtime was reportedly chosen to fit Beethoven's 9th Symphony. Over 200 billion CDs have been manufactured.

events.title: We Are the World Recorded
events.blurb: Forty-five American pop stars gathered at a Los Angeles recording studio after the annual American Music Awards ceremony to record a charity single for African famine relief, written by two headliners in a single evening. The recording session ran until 8 AM. The single sold over 20 million copies and raised more than $63 million. Its producer had hung a sign at the studio entrance reading: "Check your ego at the door."
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1985 — written by Michael Jackson and Lionel Richie; produced by Quincy Jones. Participating artists included Stevie Wonder, Bruce Springsteen, Bob Dylan, Diana Ross, and Ray Charles. The sign was Jones's idea. A 2024 Netflix documentary rehashed the making of the track.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: O.J. Simpson Verdict
events.blurb: A Los Angeles Superior Court jury, deliberating for only four hours after eleven months of testimony, found a former NFL running back and actor not guilty of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend. The verdict, announced at 10 AM Pacific time, was watched by an estimated 100 million Americans. National productivity visibly dropped during the broadcast. The decision split along racial lines: most white Americans believed him guilty; most Black Americans were skeptical of the Los Angeles police who had arrested him.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1995 — O.J. Simpson acquitted. Defense lawyers Johnnie Cochran ("If it doesn't fit, you must acquit") and Robert Shapiro. Simpson was later found liable for the deaths in a 1997 civil trial and ordered to pay $33.5 million. He died of cancer in April 2024 at 76.

events.title: Sputnik 1 Orbital Launch
events.blurb: A polished aluminum sphere the size of a beach ball lifted off from a steppe launch site and became the first human-made object to orbit Earth. Weighing 83 kilograms and trailing four whip antennas, it circled the planet every 96 minutes and broadcast a radio beep on 20 and 40 MHz audible to amateur operators worldwide for 22 days until its batteries died.
events.revealBlurb: October 4, 1957 — Sputnik 1. It carried zero scientific instruments; the entire payload was a thermometer and a radio transmitter. The beep's rhythm changed with cabin temperature, which meant the world's most-tracked signal was also the world's first space weather report.

events.title: Explorer 1 — First US Satellite
events.blurb: A Juno I rocket launched the United States' first satellite from Cape Canaveral, placing an 8.3 kg cylinder into an elliptical orbit that reached 2,550 km altitude. The satellite's Geiger–Müller tube detected a region of intense radiation surrounding Earth — data that led James Van Allen to identify the radiation belts bearing his name.
events.revealBlurb: January 31, 1958 — Explorer 1. The US had been beaten to orbit by Sputnik 1 and Sputnik 2 in the previous three months. In a press conference photo, three scientists hoisted a full-scale model over their heads in triumph — the actual satellite weighed less than a toaster oven. Explorer 1 remained in orbit for 12 years.

events.title: First Crewed Lunar Orbit
events.blurb: Three astronauts fired their Service Propulsion System engine on Christmas Eve to enter orbit 112 km above the Moon — the first humans to leave Earth's gravitational sphere of influence and orbit another world. During the mission's ninth orbit, Bill Anders photographed a crescent Earth rising over the lunar horizon, producing what became one of the most widely reproduced photographs in history.
events.revealBlurb: December 24, 1968 — Apollo 8. An estimated one billion people across 64 countries watched the Christmas Eve television broadcast in which the crew read the opening verses of Genesis. The Earthrise photograph is credited with catalyzing the environmental movement; the image appeared on the first Earth Day poster in 1970.

events.title: Apollo–Soyuz Handshake in Space
events.blurb: An American Apollo Command Module and a Soviet Soyuz spacecraft docked 225 km above the Atlantic Ocean, and their commanders exchanged the first international handshake in space through a specially built docking adapter module. The joint mission conducted five docking and undocking maneuvers and shared four crew transfer sessions over two days.
events.revealBlurb: July 17, 1975 — Apollo–Soyuz. Stafford and Leonov — who had made the first spacewalk a decade earlier — greeted each other in each other's languages. The crews exchanged seeds, flags, and medals. This was the last flight of an Apollo spacecraft and the last US human spaceflight for six years, until STS-1 in 1981.

events.title: First American Woman in Space
events.blurb: Physicist Sally Ride flew aboard Space Shuttle Challenger as a mission specialist on STS-7, becoming the first American woman and the youngest American in space at 32. The six-day mission deployed two communications satellites and was the first shuttle flight to use a robotic arm to retrieve a free-flying satellite.
events.revealBlurb: June 18, 1983 — STS-7. A reporter asked Ride before launch whether spaceflight would affect her reproductive organs; she deadpanned that no one had asked her male crewmates the same question. NASA engineers reportedly asked whether 100 tampons would be enough for the six-day flight "just to be safe." She flew again in 1984 and co-founded a science education company.

events.title: Chauvet Cave Paintings
events.blurb: Deep inside a limestone gorge in southern France, artists of the Upper Paleolithic ventured hundreds of metres into darkness with torches of burning pine and painted more than 400 animals onto the walls — rhinos, horses, cave lions, mammoths — using charcoal and red ochre. The images show sophisticated techniques: perspective, shading, motion. They would remain sealed behind a rockslide until rediscovered by three cavers in 1994.
events.revealBlurb: c. 30,000 BCE — Chauvet-Pont-d'Arc, Ardèche. Radiocarbon dating of the charcoal remains controversial; estimates span 32,000-30,000 BCE. A meticulous replica opened to tourists in 2015; the original site is restricted to scientists to preserve a fragile microclimate.

events.title: Tutankhamun Death Mask Created
events.blurb: Egyptian craftsmen fashioned a 10.2-kilogram gold funerary mask inlaid with lapis lazuli, carnelian, obsidian, and coloured glass to cover the mummy of a teenage pharaoh who had died at 18. The mask was sealed in a tomb packed with over 5,000 objects. The boy-king had been a minor figure; the tomb escaped the looting that emptied nearly every other Egyptian royal burial. It was untouched for 3,245 years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1323 BCE — Tutankhamun died. Howard Carter's team uncovered the tomb on November 4, 1922. The mask now spends most of its time in a Cairo museum case and has been on world tours twice. The beard fell off during cleaning in 2014 and was hastily reattached with epoxy.

events.title: The Last Supper Completed
events.blurb: An Italian polymath completed a 9-metre-wide mural in the refectory of a Dominican convent in a northern Italian city, depicting Christ announcing his betrayal and the instant of shocked reaction on the faces of his twelve disciples. The artist had worked on it for three years, painting in oil on a dry wall rather than true fresco — a choice that made the picture deteriorate visibly within his own lifetime.
events.revealBlurb: 1498 — Leonardo da Vinci in Santa Maria delle Grazie, Milan. His experimental technique began flaking within 20 years. The painting has been restored many times, most recently between 1978 and 1999. Allied bombing in 1943 destroyed the refectory roof but the wall survived.

events.title: Mona Lisa Stolen
events.blurb: An Italian handyman who had worked at a Paris museum hid overnight in a storage closet, walked out the next morning in his worker's smock carrying a 77 by 53 cm wooden panel under his arm, and disappeared for two years and four months. The panel was a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a Florentine merchant's wife. The theft made worldwide news; Picasso and the poet Apollinaire were briefly questioned as suspects. The picture had been little known until this moment.
events.revealBlurb: August 21, 1911 — Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence 28 months later trying to sell it to the Uffizi. He served seven months in Italian prison and was celebrated as a patriot by many Italians. The theft made the Mona Lisa internationally famous.

events.title: Banksy Shreds at Auction
events.blurb: A framed spray-painting of a girl releasing a heart-shaped balloon, sold at a London auction for £1.04 million ten seconds earlier, began to buzz mechanically and slid partway through a concealed shredder built into the custom frame. Half the canvas emerged in vertical strips; the auction house staff stared; the hammer had already fallen. The anonymous street artist who had built the device posted a video saying the mechanism was supposed to shred the whole picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 5, 2018 — Banksy, at Sotheby's London. The buyer honored the purchase. The half-shredded work was retitled "Love is in the Bin" and resold three years later for £18.6 million — 18 times the original price.

events.title: The Jazz Singer Released
events.blurb: A Warner Brothers feature film about a cantor's son who runs away to become a vaudeville singer premiered at a Times Square theatre as the first full-length motion picture with synchronized recorded dialogue. The star, in blackface for most of the film, delivered the industry's first-ever spoken movie line: "Wait a minute, wait a minute. You ain't heard nothin' yet!" Within three years almost every Hollywood film was a talkie.
events.revealBlurb: October 6, 1927 — Al Jolson at the Warners' Theatre, NYC. The film's sound system, Vitaphone, used synchronized phonograph records rather than optical audio. The silent era ended astonishingly fast; by 1930 the major Hollywood studios had written off the previous decade's technology.

events.title: The Seventh Seal Released
events.blurb: A Swedish director released a 96-minute black-and-white film about a disillusioned medieval knight, returning from the Crusades to find his homeland ravaged by plague, who plays an extended chess match with a personification of Death to postpone his own. The film's signature image — the knight and Death on a beach chessboard — entered the pantheon of instantly recognizable cinema shots, as did its bleak allegorical mode.
events.revealBlurb: February 16, 1957 — Ingmar Bergman, with Max von Sydow as the knight. The chess game has been parodied by Bill & Ted's Bogus Journey, the Muppets, and South Park, among dozens of others. Bergman wrote the screenplay in two weeks.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: Jurassic Park Released
events.blurb: A 46-year-old director released an adaptation of a recent Michael Crichton novel about genetically resurrected dinosaurs on a tropical-island theme park. The film's digital dinosaurs — only a few minutes of CGI, mixed with extensive full-size animatronic puppets — changed the calculus of what visual effects could do. Audiences gasped at a Tyrannosaurus rex roaring over a rain-soaked jeep; a decade of purely physical-effects films were obsolete.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1993 — Steven Spielberg. The T. rex breaking into the jeep was actually animatronic; it malfunctioned often in the Hawaii humidity. The film displaced E.T. as highest-grossing ever. Spielberg was editing "Schindler's List" at night during production.

events.title: The Matrix Released
events.blurb: Two siblings who had directed only one feature between them released a 136-minute science-fiction film in which the world turns out to be a computer simulation and humanity is harvested by machines as a power source. The film's "bullet time" effect — a camera arcing around a frozen-mid-action character while the world resumed behind it — became an instantly iconic technique. Its cyberpunk philosophy, couture, and green-tinted aesthetic defined the turn of the millennium.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1999 — Lana and Lilly Wachowski, starring Keanu Reeves. "Bullet time" was achieved with a ring of 120 still cameras. The concept of a simulated reality — the "red pill / blue pill" — has since migrated into every internet conspiracy subculture.

events.title: The Hijra
events.blurb: Fleeing plots against his life in the Arabian trading city where he had preached for 13 years, a 53-year-old prophet and roughly seventy of his followers slipped out at night and rode 320 kilometres north to a rival oasis town whose feuding tribes had invited him to mediate. He arrived to a welcoming reception and began building the first Islamic community under his political authority.
events.revealBlurb: July 16, 622 — Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina. The Islamic calendar begins from this year, not his birth. "Hijra" literally means "emigration" or "severing of ties."

events.title: Battle of Hastings
events.blurb: A Norman duke from across the English Channel invaded a southern English kingdom with 7,000 men, met its exhausted king — who had marched south after defeating a Norwegian invasion three weeks earlier in the north — on a hillside near the coast, and won in an all-day battle. The English king was killed, reportedly by an arrow through the eye. The victor replaced the Anglo-Saxon aristocracy with his own.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1066 — William the Conqueror vs. Harold Godwinson near the town of Battle, East Sussex. The Bayeux Tapestry, a 70-metre embroidered account, was sewn within a decade. Modern English is still 50–60 percent French-derived because of the resulting Norman elite.

events.title: Marco Polo Departs for China
events.blurb: A 17-year-old Venetian merchant's son set out with his father and uncle on a journey across Asia to the court of the Mongol emperor. He would return to Venice 24 years later and, captured in a war with Genoa three years after that, dictate an account of his travels to a cellmate. The resulting book became the most influential western description of Asia for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 1271 — Marco left Venice with Niccolò and Maffeo Polo. Returning in 1295, he was imprisoned by the Genoese; his cellmate Rustichello da Pisa helped him write "Il Milione." Christopher Columbus's annotated copy survives.

events.title: Black Death Reaches Europe
events.blurb: A plague arriving by trade galley at a Sicilian port spread through Mediterranean shipping lanes and overland caravans until, over the next five years, it killed an estimated 30-60 percent of Europe's population — perhaps 50 million people. Physicians had no effective response; flagellant processions and mass pogroms of Jews did little but spread the disease faster.
events.revealBlurb: October 1347 — Messina, Sicily. Caused by Yersinia pestis, spread by the fleas of black rats. Wages for surviving laborers roughly doubled; labor scarcity began eroding feudal obligations. The plague cycled back every decade or so for the next three centuries.

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: Great Chicago Fire
events.blurb: A fire started in a barn on a windy autumn evening in the second-largest U.S. metropolis and burned for 27 hours, destroying 17,500 buildings across 8.5 square kilometres of the central business district and killing around 300 people. A third of the city's population was left homeless.
events.revealBlurb: October 8-10, 1871 — Chicago. The Mrs. O'Leary's cow story is almost certainly a fabrication invented by a reporter who later confessed. On the very same day, the deadlier Peshtigo fire in Wisconsin killed 1,500+ people but is largely forgotten.

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Spanish Flu Pandemic Begins
events.blurb: An unusually lethal strain of influenza, carried through military camps and troop ships during the final months of a world war, infected a third of the planet and killed an estimated 50 to 100 million people in three successive waves over two years. Unlike most flus, it disproportionately killed healthy young adults by triggering cytokine storms in robust immune systems.
events.revealBlurb: March 1918 — first identified at a US Army base in Kansas. It was called "Spanish" only because wartime censorship in belligerent countries suppressed coverage; neutral Spain reported it freely, so it seemed to originate there. It had nothing to do with Spain.

events.title: Hurricane Katrina
events.blurb: A Category 3 hurricane made landfall on the US Gulf Coast, driving a storm surge that overtopped and breached the levee system protecting a major port city lying largely below sea level. 80 percent of the city flooded; 1,392 people died. The chaotic federal response — images of thousands stranded on a sports stadium roof, bodies floating in water — inflicted lasting damage on the administration in power.
events.revealBlurb: August 29, 2005 — New Orleans, Louisiana. The Superdome housed 30,000 evacuees for five days in deteriorating conditions. The head of FEMA, Michael Brown, had previously run the International Arabian Horse Association; he resigned within two weeks.

events.title: Typhoon Haiyan
events.blurb: One of the strongest tropical cyclones ever recorded at landfall — with sustained winds of 315 km/h — struck the central Philippines, obliterating coastal cities. A 7-metre storm surge drove ships onto city streets; the city of Tacloban lost most of its infrastructure. At least 6,300 people died, and 4 million were displaced.
events.revealBlurb: November 8, 2013 — Leyte province. The Filipino lead negotiator at the UN climate talks that week gave a tearful speech and began a hunger strike until "meaningful progress" was made. His country's delegation wore black.

events.title: First Birth Control Clinic
events.blurb: A public-health nurse in a Brooklyn neighbourhood of Manhattan opened a storefront clinic that distributed contraceptive information, pamphlets, and pessaries to working-class women. She had fled to Europe the previous year to escape indictment under federal obscenity laws for writing about contraception; she now dared local authorities to close her. They obliged on day nine.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1916 — Margaret Sanger in Brownsville, Brooklyn. She was jailed for 30 days. Her appeal established that doctors could legally prescribe contraception. She founded what would become Planned Parenthood a decade later.

events.title: Roe v. Wade
events.blurb: The U.S. Supreme Court ruled 7-2 that the right to privacy implicit in the 14th Amendment protected a woman's decision to terminate a pregnancy, striking down most state abortion laws. The ruling established a three-trimester framework balancing state interests against individual rights. It would remain the governing precedent for 49 years, until its overturn in 2022 returned abortion regulation to the states.
events.revealBlurb: January 22, 1973 — plaintiff "Jane Roe" was Norma McCorvey, who never actually had the abortion. She changed her position on the issue multiple times before her death in 2017. The ruling was overturned by Dobbs v. Jackson on June 24, 2022.

events.title: Sandra Day O'Connor Confirmed
events.blurb: A 51-year-old former state senator and state appellate judge from the American Southwest was confirmed by the U.S. Senate 99-0 as the first woman to sit on the U.S. Supreme Court, fulfilling a campaign promise the president who had nominated her made during the 1980 election. She would serve 24 years, writing decisions on affirmative action, abortion, and the disputed 2000 election.
events.revealBlurb: September 21, 1981 — confirmed; Ronald Reagan had nominated her. Her 2005 retirement was precipitated by her husband's declining health from Alzheimer's. She herself was diagnosed with dementia in 2018 and died in 2023.

events.title: Anita Hill Testifies
events.blurb: A 35-year-old law professor at a large university in the central U.S., subpoenaed by the Senate Judiciary Committee considering a Supreme Court nomination, testified publicly on live television that the nominee — her former supervisor at a federal agency — had sexually harassed her nearly a decade earlier. The all-male Senate committee confirmed him anyway by a 52-48 vote. The hearings galvanized a wave of women candidates; 47 won congressional seats the following year.
events.revealBlurb: October 11-13, 1991 — Hill testified against Clarence Thomas. Thomas was confirmed October 15 and is still on the Court. The 1992 elections were dubbed "the Year of the Woman" — though they still left women only 10 percent of Congress.

events.title: #MeToo Goes Viral
events.blurb: Five days after a major U.S. newspaper published a long investigation into sexual harassment and assault allegations against a powerful Hollywood film producer, an actress posted on Twitter asking women who had been sexually harassed or assaulted to reply with two words. Within 24 hours, those two words had been used 500,000 times on Twitter alone. The phrase had been coined a decade earlier by a Black activist working with survivors in the American South.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 2017 — Alyssa Milano's tweet; the phrase was coined in 2006 by Tarana Burke. The producer was Harvey Weinstein, finally convicted of rape in February 2020. A cascade of resignations, prosecutions, and cultural reckoning followed across industries.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: Kismet Released
events.blurb: A Bombay Talkies crime film with an unambiguous anti-hero — the lead character is a thief and a cad — opened in the depths of winter during a bitter internal dispute that was tearing the studio apart, yet became the first film in Indian cinema history to gross ₹1 crore. At a Calcutta cinema it ran for 187 consecutive weeks, a record that stood for 32 years.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 1943, Bombay. Directed by Gyan Mukherjee, starring Ashok Kumar. Its patriotic song "Door Hato Ae Duniyawalon" — aimed at colonial occupation without naming it — spread through cities as independence agitation intensified. The British censors initially approved it without grasping the subtext.

events.title: Awaara Released
events.blurb: A Raj Kapoor crime drama about a judge's illegitimate son — playing on the 1940s debate over heredity versus environment — became India's highest-grossing domestic release of the year and then, when dubbed and released abroad three years later, drew 64 million viewers in the Soviet Union alone, a record for any foreign film in that market. Its theme song became a street-singing anthem across Eurasia.
events.revealBlurb: December 14, 1951 — Raj Kapoor directed and starred. The song "Awaara Hoon" was so popular in the USSR, Turkey, and China that Soviet children grew up singing it phonetically in Hindi. Kapoor was reportedly stopped in Moscow streets for autographs.

events.title: First National Film Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: India's first government-adjudicated film awards were presented at Vigyan Bhavan in New Delhi by the President of the Republic, honouring the best films of 1953 across features, documentaries, and children's cinema. The ceremony established that Indian cinema was not merely entertainment but a matter of national cultural policy — a position that has shaped every film ministry since.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 1954. First Best Feature Film: Shyamchi Aai, a Marathi film about maternal devotion — not a Bombay product, a signal about the awards' intent to honour all Indian languages. The ceremony was conceived explicitly to reward what the state considered the right kind of cinema.

events.title: Jawan Released
events.blurb: A Tamil director's Hindi-film debut — a dual-role action thriller mixing vigilante politics with hospital corruption — earned ₹75 crore on its opening day, making it the highest-opening-day gross in Hindi cinema at the time, then crossed ₹600 crore domestically, becoming the first Hindi film to do so. Its release capped a year in which its star reclaimed the top of the industry after a decade's absence.
events.revealBlurb: September 7, 2023 — directed by Atlee. Shah Rukh Khan's return, following Pathaan earlier that year, made 2023 the most commercially dominant single-year performance by any one actor in Bollywood history. The film's opening credits featured cameos by over thirty prominent South Indian actors.

events.title: Partition of Bengal
events.blurb: A British viceroy, citing administrative efficiency, split a vast eastern province of colonial India into two along religious lines — a Muslim-majority east and a Hindu-majority west — over the fierce protests of its Bengali elite. Boycotts of British goods, the Swadeshi movement, and targeted assassinations followed. The partition was reversed six years later, but the communal logic it had introduced could not be uninvented.
events.revealBlurb: October 16, 1905 — announced by Lord Curzon. Rabindranath Tagore led Hindus and Muslims in tying rakhis on each other's wrists in protest. The reunification in 1911 coincided with moving the colonial capital from Calcutta to Delhi.

events.title: Jallianwala Bagh Massacre
events.blurb: A British brigadier-general marched 50 rifle-armed soldiers into a walled garden in a Punjabi city where thousands of Sikhs, Hindus, and Muslims had gathered for a spring harvest festival. Without warning, he ordered ten minutes of continuous fire into the unarmed crowd, ceasing only when ammunition ran low. Official counts put the dead at 379; Indian sources gave over 1,000. He was celebrated in parts of British society as a saviour of empire.
events.revealBlurb: April 13, 1919 — Amritsar, Baisakhi day. Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer. The poet Rabindranath Tagore renounced his British knighthood in protest. A young Sikh named Udham Singh, who was at the garden that day, assassinated the former lieutenant-governor responsible for the region 21 years later in London.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Babri Masjid Demolition
events.blurb: A mob of around 150,000 Hindu nationalists who had gathered for what was officially billed as a symbolic prayer ceremony at a disputed 16th-century mosque in a north Indian town overpowered the police cordon and demolished the structure with pickaxes and crowbars over six hours. Riots across the country in the following weeks killed 2,000 people, mostly Muslims. A Hindu temple now stands on the site, inaugurated 31 years later.
events.revealBlurb: December 6, 1992 — Ayodhya. The Supreme Court ruled in 2019 that the demolition was illegal, but awarded the site to the Hindu temple trust. The Ram Mandir was consecrated on January 22, 2024.

events.title: Right to Information Act
events.blurb: A law guaranteeing any citizen of the country the right to request information from public authorities — and compelling officials to respond within 30 days or face personal penalties — came into force after a decade-long campaign driven by rural social movements in a western state. It quickly became one of the most-used such laws in the world, exposing corruption from village panchayats to the prime minister's office.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 2005 — RTI Act. Aruna Roy's Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan was the movement's backbone. Its origins lay in drought-era sit-ins demanding to see the village wage registers. More than a hundred RTI activists have been murdered since passage.

events.title: Columbus Makes Landfall
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator commanding three vessels landed on an island in the present-day Bahamas after 70 days at sea, believing he had reached islands off the coast of Asia. He planted a royal standard, claimed the land in the name of the Spanish Crown, and named the island San Salvador — its indigenous inhabitants called it Guanahani.

events.title: Vasco da Gama Reaches India
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Portuguese captain, after a 10-month voyage south around the southern tip of Africa and up its eastern coast, dropped anchor at a spice port on the Malabar coast of India. He had sailed further than any previous European expedition. The local ruler was unimpressed by the trinkets he offered as tribute, but the sea route to Asian spices — breaking the Venetian and Arab overland monopoly — was now open.
events.revealBlurb: May 20, 1498 — Vasco da Gama at Calicut (Kozhikode), India. His expedition had left Lisbon with 170 men; 54 returned alive. He would make two more voyages and die in India in 1524 as the country's viceroy.

events.title: Jamestown Colony Founded
events.blurb: English settlers dispatched by the Virginia Company came ashore on a low, marshy peninsula in the tidewater and drove stakes for the first permanent English settlement in the territory that would become the United States. Of the roughly 104 men and boys who arrived, fewer than 40 survived their first year, undone by brackish drinking water, starvation, and disease.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1607 — Virginia. The site was chosen partly because its deep water let ships dock without anchors — and partly because it looked easy to defend. It was also mosquito-ridden and had no fresh water. Within nine months, roughly 65% of the colonists were dead.

events.title: Mayflower Compact Signed
events.blurb: 41 male passengers of a merchant ship that had landed at the wrong spot on the Massachusetts coast — they had intended the Hudson River — signed a short agreement on the ship to govern themselves by the will of the majority until permanent civil authority could be established. The document was pragmatic, not ideological, but became a foundational text of American self-government. The Pilgrims who signed it were fleeing religious persecution in England via the Netherlands.
events.revealBlurb: November 11, 1620 (Old Style) / November 21, 1620 (New Style) — aboard the Mayflower, Cape Cod. Half the colony's 102 passengers died of scurvy and starvation the first winter. The autumn 1621 harvest feast with the Wampanoag is the ancestor of the American Thanksgiving.

events.title: Bacon's Novum Organum
events.blurb: A 59-year-old English Lord Chancellor published a Latin treatise proposing a new method for the natural sciences — not the deduction from first principles that Aristotelian scholars had relied on for eighteen centuries, but the patient inductive accumulation of observations, cataloguing of anomalies, and testing of hypotheses. The method he described, refined and formalized over the next century, became recognizable as the modern scientific method.
events.revealBlurb: 1620 — Francis Bacon, "Novum Organum Scientiarum." He was dismissed from the Lord Chancellorship the next year for taking bribes. He died in 1626 after catching pneumonia from stuffing a chicken with snow to study the preservation of meat — an early experimental death.

events.title: Great Pyramid of Giza Completed
events.blurb: A vast limestone monument covering 5.3 hectares and rising 146 metres — the tallest man-made structure for 3,800 years — was completed as the royal tomb of the second king of Egypt's Fourth Dynasty. It consists of 2.3 million blocks, each weighing 2.5 tonnes on average, quarried from nearby escarpments and shipped down the Nile. Some 20,000 paid labourers — not slaves, as was long assumed — built it in roughly twenty years.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2560 BCE — Pharaoh Khufu (Cheops). It was originally clad in smooth white limestone, robbed mostly in medieval times for Cairo construction. Its internal geometry — chambers, passages, "air shafts" — continues to attract theorizing. It is the last surviving "Seven Wonders of the Ancient World."

events.title: Pont du Gard Built
events.blurb: A three-tiered limestone aqueduct bridge was constructed to carry water 50 kilometres across southern Gaul to the Roman colony of Nemausus (modern Nîmes). The top level — 48 metres above the River Gard — still carried its channel; the whole structure spans 275 metres. It was built dry, without mortar, using stones so precisely cut that the joints remain watertight after two millennia. The aqueduct itself was decommissioned in the 6th century; the bridge survived as a road crossing.
events.revealBlurb: c. 50 CE — built under Emperor Claudius. The water it carried had a gradient of only 1 in 3,000 — about 30 centimetres of drop per kilometre. The Pont du Gard is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the most visited tourist destinations in France.

events.title: Forbidden City Completed
events.blurb: A Ming-dynasty emperor completed an imperial palace complex at the center of his new northern capital — 980 buildings, 9,999 rooms, on a site of 72 hectares, enclosed by a moat and a 10-metre wall. It served as the home and ceremonial centre of 24 successive emperors across two dynasties. The compound was closed to the public for 500 years; it was opened as a museum after the abdication of the last Qing emperor in 1912.
events.revealBlurb: 1420 — the Yongle Emperor, completing the move of the Ming capital from Nanjing to Beijing. Over a million workers built it in 14 years. The last emperor to live there was Puyi, who was expelled in 1924. It is now China's most-visited museum.

events.title: Brunelleschi's Dome Completed
events.blurb: A Florentine goldsmith turned architect completed, after 16 years of work without scaffolding, a vast octagonal dome over the crossing of a century-old cathedral. The double-shelled design, assembled with four million bricks in a self-supporting herringbone pattern, spanned 42 metres — wider than any dome built since Roman antiquity. The cathedral had stood domeless for over a century, waiting for someone to figure out how.
events.revealBlurb: August 25, 1436 — consecrated. Filippo Brunelleschi at Santa Maria del Fiore, Florence. He refused to leave blueprints, fearing competitors would steal the ideas. Part of the technique was rediscovered only in the 20th century through forensic study of the bricks.

events.title: Sydney Opera House Opens
events.blurb: A sail-shaped performing-arts complex on a harbour peninsula opened after 14 years of construction — ten times its original budget and nine years late. The Danish architect had won the design competition in 1957 but resigned in 1966 after political attacks and budget fights; he never saw the completed building. Its concrete "sails," covered in a million tiles of two shades of white, immediately made it one of the most recognized buildings in the world.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1973 — architect Jørn Utzon; opened by Queen Elizabeth II. Utzon was eventually reconciled with the building in 1999, 25 years after he left; he was awarded the Pritzker Prize in 2003 but never saw the interior of his own building. It is now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.title: First Public Film Screening
events.blurb: Two French brothers, sons of a portrait photographer, held the first commercial screening of projected motion pictures in the basement of a Paris café. The audience of 33 paid one franc each to watch ten short films — workers leaving a factory, a baby being fed, a boat leaving a harbor. Their cinematograph was both camera and projector; the film was 35mm. Within a year their operators were touring every continent.
events.revealBlurb: December 28, 1895 — Louis and Auguste Lumière at the Salon Indien du Grand Café, Paris. The apocryphal story that audiences ran screaming from the train-arriving film comes from a later screening. The Lumières thought cinema was "an invention without a future" and quickly moved on to other projects.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: The Godfather Released
events.blurb: A 32-year-old American director of partial Italian descent, working on his third feature, released a 175-minute adaptation of a recent mass-market novel about an Italian-American crime family. His studio had imposed cast, budget, and length conditions throughout production; it had also tried to fire him multiple times. The film grossed more than any previous picture in history, won Best Picture, and launched decades of imitators that have never quite matched it.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1972 — Francis Ford Coppola. Marlon Brando's sagging jowls were created with dental plumpers; Al Pacino's casting was fought bitterly by Paramount executives who wanted Ryan O'Neal. The horse's head was real — acquired from a dog-food plant.

events.title: Pulp Fiction Released
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American director released a 154-minute crime picture with a deliberately non-linear structure, three loosely interwoven storylines, and dialogue about hamburgers, foot massages, and divine intervention. It had cost $8 million, been passed on by multiple studios, and been rescued by a new boutique distributor. It won the top prize at Cannes, grossed over $200 million, and pulled a whole generation of independent filmmakers into its wake.
events.revealBlurb: October 14, 1994 — Quentin Tarantino, released by Miramax. The opening Cannes screening received a 15-minute standing ovation. John Travolta's comeback, the soundtrack's surf-rock revival, and the dance scene became instant cultural touchstones.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.

events.title: Cyrus the Great Takes Babylon
events.blurb: A Persian king who had already conquered Media, Lydia, and the Ionian cities entered the ancient city of Babylon without a fight, claiming to have been welcomed by its priests as the rightful king of the gods. His subsequent proclamation — known from a surviving cuneiform cylinder — repatriated exiled populations, restored local temples, and is sometimes described as the oldest surviving charter of human rights. The Persian Achaemenid Empire he founded became the largest the world had yet seen.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 539 BCE — Cyrus II. The Cyrus Cylinder is now in the British Museum. The Hebrew Bible credits Cyrus with allowing the Judean exiles to return to Jerusalem and rebuild the Temple; he is the only non-Jewish figure called "messiah" in the Hebrew scriptures.

events.title: Battle of Salamis
events.blurb: A Greek allied fleet of roughly 370 triremes, lured into position by a false message from the Athenian commander, engaged a Persian fleet of perhaps 800 in the narrow straits between a small island and the Athenian mainland coast. The Persian ships, crowded in the strait, could not maneuver; the Greek triremes rammed them methodically for twelve hours. Over 200 Persian ships were sunk or captured. The Persian king watched the disaster unfold from a throne on the adjacent mainland.
events.revealBlurb: September 480 BCE — Themistocles, Athenian strategos. The Persian king was Xerxes I; he retreated to Asia with much of his army, leaving a smaller force that was destroyed at Plataea the following year. Aeschylus, who had fought at Salamis himself, wrote a play about it eight years later.

events.title: Alexander the Great Dies
events.blurb: A 32-year-old conqueror, having created an empire stretching from Macedonia to northwestern India in ten years of campaigning, died of fever (or poisoning — sources disagree) in a palace in a Mesopotamian capital while planning the next campaign, this one against Arabia. He left no clear heir; his generals divided the empire into warring successor states — the Hellenistic kingdoms — that shaped Mediterranean culture for the next three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: June 10 or 11, 323 BCE — Alexander III in Babylon. Asked on his deathbed to whom his empire should go, he reportedly said: "To the strongest." Competing theories for his death: malaria, typhoid, alcoholism, West Nile virus, poisoning by his general Antipater. His body was hijacked en route home by Ptolemy to Alexandria.

events.title: Hannibal Crosses the Alps
events.blurb: A 29-year-old Carthaginian general marched an army of 50,000 men, 9,000 cavalry, and 37 war elephants from Iberia over the Alps into northern Italy over 15 days of early winter, intending to take the war to Rome's home territory. Half his men died in the crossing from cold, hunger, and hostile Alpine tribes. The force that did make it to Italy shocked Rome by winning three successive battles within two years, annihilating Roman legions at Trebbia, Lake Trasimene, and Cannae.
events.revealBlurb: 218 BCE — Hannibal Barca. The exact Alpine pass he used is still debated; the leading candidates are the Col de la Traversette or the Col du Mont Cenis. Only a few elephants made it across and most died in Italy's wet winter. Hannibal won tactically but could not take Rome itself.

events.title: Battle of the Catalaunian Plains
events.blurb: A Roman general of Germanic birth led a coalition of Romans, Visigoths, Franks, Burgundians, and Alans against a massive Hunnic invasion of Gaul under their formidable king. The battle — one of the largest ever fought in antiquity — ended in an indecisive but bloody Roman-allied victory that stopped the Huns' westward expansion. The Hunnic king would die suddenly two years later on his wedding night from a burst blood vessel; his empire collapsed within a decade.
events.revealBlurb: 451 CE — Flavius Aetius (Roman) and Theodoric I (Visigoth) vs. Attila the Hun. Theodoric was killed in the battle. Attila's death in 453, on his wedding night to a Germanic princess named Ildico, was probably from an esophageal hemorrhage. His sons squabbled; the Hunnic Empire dissolved.

events.title: Altair 8800 Released
events.blurb: A cover article in an American hobbyist electronics magazine featured a $397 kit-build computer based on the Intel 8080 microprocessor, aimed at hardware enthusiasts willing to solder circuit boards and toggle binary instructions with front-panel switches. The magazine received over 2,000 kit orders in the first month. Among the Harvard students who saw the cover and wrote a BASIC interpreter for the machine were Bill Gates and Paul Allen.
events.revealBlurb: January 1975 — MITS Altair 8800, on the cover of Popular Electronics. Gates and Allen's BASIC would become the founding product of Microsoft. The Altair is universally credited as the first commercially successful microcomputer.

events.title: Apple II Released
events.blurb: A young Californian computer company released their second machine — and the first mass-market personal computer designed for non-hobbyists, with built-in color graphics, a working keyboard, a plastic case, and the ability to display text and graphics simultaneously. It shipped for $1,298 and found a broad market among small businesses, schools, and households. Apple's revenues grew 700 percent a year for five consecutive years.
events.revealBlurb: June 10, 1977 — Apple Computer. Engineered largely by Steve Wozniak. The arrival of VisiCalc two years later made it the first computer that small businesses felt they had to buy. Apple sold over 5 million Apple IIs before discontinuing the line in 1993.

events.title: iPod Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company released a white portable music player with a 5 GB hard drive — "1,000 songs in your pocket," according to its co-founder's introduction — and a scrollwheel for navigation. The industry press was unimpressed; smaller MP3 players already existed. Over the next decade, the iPod and its derivatives would sell over 400 million units, reshape the music industry, and serve as a forerunner and technological foundation for the iPhone.
events.revealBlurb: October 23, 2001 — Apple iPod. Steve Jobs introduced it at a small press event, not to a large keynote crowd. Initial reviews focused on how it was Mac-only; the 2003 Windows version opened the floodgates.

events.title: iPhone Announced
events.blurb: A California computer company's co-founder unveiled a new class of mobile phone at a San Francisco conference, combining a widescreen iPod, a mobile internet browser, and a phone into a single slim device controlled entirely by a multi-touch finger-driven screen. He dialled a coffee shop on stage to demonstrate. Nokia's executives watching the announcement reportedly laughed at its lack of a physical keyboard; BlackBerry's CEO later admitted they also underestimated it.
events.revealBlurb: January 9, 2007 — Steve Jobs at Macworld. It went on sale June 29. The original did not support 3G, had no copy-and-paste, and shipped without an App Store — those all came in subsequent years. Apple now makes over $200 billion a year just from iPhones.

events.title: First Android Phone Released
events.blurb: A Taiwanese handset maker released the first commercial phone running an open-source mobile operating system developed by a Silicon Valley search-engine company, available through a US mobile carrier. The device had a physical keyboard that slid out from under the screen; unlike the rival iPhone, users could install apps from anywhere, replace the default apps, and generally modify the device at will. Open-ecosystem Android would grow to dominate global smartphone market share.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 2008 — T-Mobile G1 (HTC Dream), running Android 1.0. Google had quietly acquired Android Inc. for $50 million in 2005. By 2013 more than half of smartphones sold ran Android; today it's over 70 percent globally.

events.title: Epic of Gilgamesh Compiled
events.blurb: Mesopotamian scribes compiled the standard version of a long cuneiform poem about a semi-legendary king of a Sumerian city, his wild-man companion, and a flood survivor they visit in search of immortality. Earlier Sumerian poems about the hero had been circulating for centuries; a single scribe, working in Akkadian, produced the integrated twelve-tablet version that survives. It is the oldest recognized work of narrative literature.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1200 BCE — standard Babylonian version attributed to the scribe Sin-liqe-unninni. The poem's flood narrative preceded the one in Genesis by at least 500 years. Rediscovered in fragments in 19th-century excavations of Nineveh.

events.title: One Thousand and One Nights Compiled
events.blurb: An anonymous Arabic compiler assembled a frame narrative and embedded stories drawn from Persian, Indian, Mesopotamian, and Egyptian sources into a single cycle. The outer frame told of a queen stalling her own execution by telling her king a new story every night; the inner tales — of flying carpets, genies, thieves — became permanent fixtures of world storytelling. The collection continued to accrete new tales for centuries.
events.revealBlurb: c. 10th century CE — the oldest surviving Arabic manuscript dates from the 14th century. "Aladdin," "Ali Baba," and "Sinbad" were added to the collection by an 18th-century French translator, Antoine Galland, working from Syrian oral sources. They are not in the original Arabic canon.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Printed
events.blurb: A goldsmith in a Rhine-valley city completed the first book printed in Europe using movable metal type — a Latin Bible set in 42 lines per page, bound in 180 copies. His press combined existing technologies — oil-based ink, a wine-press frame, cast-metal punches — into an invention that would be blamed for everything from the Reformation to the Renaissance to modern literacy.
events.revealBlurb: 1455 — Johannes Gutenberg in Mainz. Forty-nine copies are known to survive; roughly twenty are complete. Gutenberg himself was sued by his financier the same year and lost the press.

events.title: Moby-Dick Published
events.blurb: A 31-year-old American novelist published his sixth novel — a 135-chapter whaling yarn interleaved with encyclopedic digressions on cetacean anatomy, metaphysical speculation, and a revenge monomania culminating in an apocalyptic confrontation with a great white whale. The book sold 3,215 copies in its first 18 months and then essentially nothing for decades. The author died largely forgotten. The rediscovery of the novel's greatness did not come until the 1920s.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1851 — Herman Melville. The white whale was loosely based on a real albino sperm whale, Mocha Dick, which reportedly stove in ships. The book was first published in London as "The Whale"; the American edition restored the title "Moby-Dick; or, The Whale."

events.title: Rabindranath Tagore Wins Nobel
events.blurb: A 52-year-old Bengali polymath — poet, novelist, philosopher, composer, painter — was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature, becoming the first non-European and the first Asian to receive the honour. The Swedish Academy specifically cited his English translation of his own Bengali poetry collection "Gitanjali." The award brought him international fame; at home in colonial India it cemented him as a national cultural figure.
events.revealBlurb: November 13, 1913 — Rabindranath Tagore. He renounced his British knighthood in 1919 after the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre. He composed the national anthems of both India ("Jana Gana Mana") and Bangladesh ("Amar Shonar Bangla"), two of three anthems he wrote for different countries.

events.title: Declaration of Independence Adopted
events.blurb: Delegates from thirteen British colonies voted to ratify a document asserting that all men are created equal and endowed with unalienable rights, formally severing political ties with the Crown. The declaration listed 27 specific grievances against the king; most delegates signed an engrossed parchment copy nearly a month later.
events.revealBlurb: July 4, 1776 — Philadelphia. Only two men actually signed on the Fourth (Hancock and Thomson). Jefferson, Franklin, and Adams all died on July 4 — Jefferson and Adams on the same day, the 50th anniversary, within hours of each other.

events.title: British Surrender at Saratoga
events.blurb: A British army of 6,000 men under a genteel general who had marched south from Canada intending to split the American colonies along the Hudson Valley found itself encircled at a rural New York hamlet after two pitched battles and dwindling supplies. The general surrendered his entire force to the American commander. It was the most consequential Allied success of the war; France, which had been secretly aiding the colonies, publicly entered the conflict four months later.
events.revealBlurb: October 17, 1777 — British general John Burgoyne surrenders to American general Horatio Gates. Burgoyne had been marching from Canada; a complementary British push up the Hudson from New York had been misdirected to Pennsylvania. The victory secured French diplomatic recognition and military alliance.

events.title: Napoleon Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Corsican-born general, having ruled France as First Consul for five years, staged a coronation at the Gothic cathedral in the French capital. He had negotiated the pope's attendance; in the ceremony's most famous moment — possibly prearranged, possibly improvised — the emperor took the crown from the pope and placed it on his own head. The act was read as a message: no religious authority ratified his power.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1804 — Notre-Dame de Paris. Pope Pius VII had been brought from Rome; he sat largely passive through the ceremony. Napoleon's wife Joséphine also crowned herself empress. Jacques-Louis David's monumental painting of the coronation, finished three years later, flatters Napoleon's height among other details.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: Battle of Leipzig
events.blurb: Four days of fighting around a Saxon city produced the largest battle in European history before World War I, with 600,000 men engaged. A coalition of Russian, Austrian, Prussian, and Swedish forces defeated Napoleon's Grand Army, pressuring a French retreat west over the Rhine. Napoleon had lost Germany; he would lose France within six months. The battle is known in Germany as the Battle of the Nations.
events.revealBlurb: October 16-19, 1813 — Leipzig, Saxony. Casualties: perhaps 100,000 total — roughly 38,000 French, 54,000 Allied. The Battle of Trafalgar eight years earlier had ended French naval power; Leipzig ended French land dominance.

events.title: Founding of Rome
events.blurb: According to Roman tradition, Romulus killed his twin brother Remus in a quarrel over the city's walls, then became the first king of a settlement of seven hills beside the Tiber. Varro, working backward from consular lists, calculated the exact date centuries later and Rome adopted it as its birthday, celebrating it annually with the Parilia festival.
events.revealBlurb: April 21, 753 BCE — the traditional date. Romulus allegedly populated his new city by opening it as a sanctuary for fugitives, runaway slaves, and exiles. When women were in short supply, he invited the neighbouring Sabines to a festival and had his men abduct their daughters.

events.title: Battle of Zama
events.blurb: Scipio Africanus neutralised Hannibal's 80 war elephants by opening lanes in his formation so they stampeded harmlessly through, then used superior cavalry to encircle the Carthaginian infantry. Roughly 20,000 Carthaginians died; Carthage accepted a peace stripping it of its fleet, all war elephants, and 10,000 silver talents paid over fifty years.
events.revealBlurb: October 19, 202 BCE, North Africa. This was the only time in Hannibal's career that his battle plan failed. After the war, Scipio received the cognomen "Africanus"; his grateful soldiers offered to make him king of Rome, which he refused.

events.title: Beginning of the Crisis of the Third Century
events.blurb: The assassination of Emperor Severus Alexander by his own troops triggered nearly fifty years of catastrophic instability: more than twenty emperors in half a century, nearly all killed by soldiers or rivals, with simultaneous invasions across every frontier and a fragmenting empire that briefly split into three competing states. The population and economy contracted severely.
events.revealBlurb: 235 CE, Germany. Maximinus Thrax, the soldier who replaced Severus Alexander, was reportedly 8 feet tall and drank a wheelbarrow's worth of water per day — details that are almost certainly exaggerated. He never visited Rome during his three-year reign and was killed by his own troops outside Aquileia.

events.title: Aurelian Reunifies the Empire
events.blurb: After the empire had fractured into three competing states, Emperor Aurelian defeated the Palmyrene Empire in the east — capturing its queen Zenobia — and then the breakaway Gallic Empire in the west, bringing Britain, Gaul, Spain, Syria, and Egypt back under a single ruler within five years of taking power. He then began building a massive new defensive wall around Rome itself.
events.revealBlurb: 274 CE. Queen Zenobia of Palmyra had claimed descent from Cleopatra and ruled a sophisticated court of scholars and poets while commanding legions across the Near East. After capture she was eventually settled near Tivoli and, according to some sources, married a Roman senator.

events.title: Attila Invades Italy
events.blurb: Hunnic forces under Attila crossed the Alps, razed the wealthy port city of Aquileia so completely it was never rebuilt, and sacked Milan and Pavia before advancing toward Rome itself. Pope Leo I led a diplomatic mission to meet Attila on the banks of the Mincio River; Attila withdrew without attacking Rome, though historians debate whether Leo, disease, famine, or approaching eastern armies deserved the credit.
events.revealBlurb: Summer 452 CE. Aquileia had been one of the richest cities in the western empire; legend says its refugees founded Venice on the lagoon islands to escape the Huns. Attila died the following year on his wedding night — of a nosebleed, according to ancient sources.

events.title: Mother India Released
events.blurb: A near-three-hour epic about a village woman who spends decades breaking stones, raising sons, and protecting her community from a money-lender opened on Diwali across India and broke every box-office record to that point. The following year it became India's first film nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film — losing by a single vote to a Federico Fellini picture.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1957. Directed by Mehboob Khan. Nargis, who plays the mother, married co-star Sunil Dutt after he dragged her unconscious from a fire that broke out on set. Khan's production logo featured a hammer-and-sickle; it was quietly removed before the Oscar submission print.

events.title: Zanjeer Released
events.blurb: After fifteen consecutive flops, a young actor was offered the role of an angry, incorruptible police inspector in a crime thriller that every major star of the decade — Dharmendra, Dev Anand, Rajesh Khanna — had turned down. The film's success redirected an entire industry's idea of what a Hindi film hero could look like: not romantic or comic, but furious.
events.revealBlurb: May 11, 1973 — written by Salim-Javed, directed by Prakash Mehra. Amitabh Bachchan was cast almost by elimination. Salim Khan and Javed Akhtar then wrote nearly every subsequent Bachchan blockbuster with him specifically in mind, insisting on his casting as a contractual condition.

events.title: Bobby Released
events.blurb: A teen romance between a rich Hindu boy and a poor Goan Christian fisherman's daughter — directed by a father launching his second son into stardom — upended Bollywood's existing template of adult romances and star-crossed melodrama. The film's bikini-clad poster and youth-coded aesthetics signalled an entirely new demographic that filmmakers had been ignoring.
events.revealBlurb: September 29, 1973 — Raj Kapoor directing Rishi Kapoor in his leading-role debut, opposite Dimple Kapadia in hers. The film became the highest-grossing of 1973. Raj Kapoor cast Dimple Kapadia after seeing her at a party; she was sixteen. She married Rajesh Khanna five months after filming wrapped.

events.title: Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge Released
events.blurb: A romance about two Non-Resident Indians falling in love on a Eurorail trip before battling parental disapproval opened in Bombay that autumn and never fully left: it ran continuously at one Mumbai cinema for over two decades, setting a record no Indian film has matched. Its climactic train-platform scene became shorthand for every subsequent Bollywood love story.
events.revealBlurb: October 20, 1995 — Aditya Chopra's directorial debut, age 23. He refused to watch the film with an audience for years. Shah Rukh Khan initially had reservations about the role. The film ran at Mumbai's Maratha Mandir theatre without interruption until 2023 — 1,278 weeks.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: Fulton's Clermont Steamboat
events.blurb: A 41-year-old American engineer piloted a 40-metre paddlewheel steamboat he had built with financing from a New York politician 240 kilometres up the Hudson River from New York City to Albany, against the current, in 32 hours — a trip that had previously taken sailing sloops four days. The voyage proved steam-powered river transport commercially viable, revolutionizing inland commerce across the newly expanded United States.
events.revealBlurb: August 17, 1807 — Robert Fulton's Clermont. Spectators along the riverbanks initially took the steam-belching boat for a dragon. Fulton held a 30-year steamboat monopoly on New York waters, broken by the 1824 Supreme Court case Gibbons v. Ogden, which is still taught in law schools.

events.title: Rocket Wins the Rainhill Trials
events.blurb: A north-west English railway company held a ten-day public competition to choose the locomotive type for its forthcoming long-distance line between two major industrial cities. Five entries competed; three broke down. A machine designed by a railway engineer and his son, weighing 4.3 tonnes and achieving a top speed of 48 km/h, won the £500 prize and the contract. It was the model for every subsequent steam locomotive.
events.revealBlurb: October 6-14, 1829 — George and Robert Stephenson's "Rocket" at Rainhill, between Liverpool and Manchester. Its multi-tube boiler was the design insight; earlier engines had used single large flues and wasted heat. The Rocket is preserved at London's Science Museum.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Benz Patents the Motorwagen
events.blurb: A 41-year-old German mechanical engineer filed a patent for a three-wheeled vehicle powered by a single-cylinder internal combustion engine of his own design. The machine, producing about 2/3 of a horsepower, could reach a top speed of 16 km/h. His wife Bertha took it on an unauthorized 106-kilometre cross-country trip two years later without telling him, demonstrating its practicality; the publicity helped launch the commercial automobile industry.
events.revealBlurb: January 29, 1886 — Karl Benz, Mannheim. Bertha's 1888 trip required her to refuel at apothecaries (selling ligroin, a cleaning solvent, as the only available fuel) and improvise brake repairs using her garter as an insulator. Benz's company later merged with Daimler's to form Mercedes-Benz.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: U-2 Incident
events.blurb: A high-altitude American reconnaissance aircraft was shot down deep inside Soviet territory by a surface-to-air missile. The CIA assumed the pilot was dead and issued a cover story about a weather research flight gone astray. Then Khrushchev triumphantly produced the pilot alive and the wreckage intact, humiliating the U.S. president on the eve of a Paris summit.
events.revealBlurb: May 1, 1960 — pilot Francis Gary Powers ejected over Sverdlovsk (now Yekaterinburg). He was traded two years later for Soviet spy Rudolf Abel on Berlin's Glienicke Bridge — the same swap dramatized in "Bridge of Spies."

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis Address
events.blurb: An American president delivered a 17-minute televised address revealing that Soviet nuclear missiles had been discovered on a Caribbean island 145 kilometres from Florida, demanding their removal within a strict deadline. The 13-day standoff that followed was the closest the Cold War came to nuclear exchange, with submarines on both sides carrying armed torpedoes.

events.title: Cuban Missile Crisis: JFK Announces Naval Blockade
events.blurb: On the 22nd of that month, President John F. Kennedy delivered a nationally televised address revealing that U.S. reconnaissance aircraft had discovered Soviet nuclear missile installations under construction in Cuba — 90 miles from Florida — and announcing a naval "quarantine" to prevent further weapons deliveries.
