For 13 days, the United States and Soviet Union stood closer to nuclear war than at any other moment in history before or since.
events.revealBlurb: October 22, 1962 — Washington, D.C. Kennedy called it a "quarantine" because a blockade is an act of war under international law. Soviet ships turned around on October 24. The secret resolution involved the U.S. quietly removing its Jupiter missiles from Turkey — a concession Kennedy couldn't publicly acknowledge for decades.

events.title: Moscow Olympics Boycott
events.blurb: Sixty-six nations, led by the United States, refused to send athletes to the Summer Games held in the Soviet capital, protesting the invasion of a neighboring country five months earlier. Eighty nations competed anyway — the smallest field since 1956. Four years later, the Soviet bloc returned the favor by boycotting the Los Angeles Games.
events.revealBlurb: July 19, 1980 — the boycott was announced by Jimmy Carter. British athletes defied their own government and competed under the Olympic flag. The 1984 Soviet retaliation cost American sprinter Evelyn Ashford a likely gold-medal duel.

events.title: KAL 007 Shot Down
events.blurb: A Korean civilian airliner carrying 269 passengers and crew strayed over Soviet airspace over the Sea of Japan on a flight from New York to Seoul. A Sukhoi interceptor fired two air-to-air missiles and the 747 broke apart over international waters. The Kremlin at first denied any involvement; the United States released taped radio transmissions of the shootdown within a week.
events.revealBlurb: September 1, 1983 — a U.S. congressman, Larry McDonald, was among the dead. Reagan called it an "act of barbarism." The incident led directly to the U.S. decision to make GPS available for civilian use, so no passenger aircraft would ever again stray for lack of navigation.

events.title: Lend-Lease Act Signed
events.blurb: A nation officially at peace passed legislation allowing its president to lend, lease, or otherwise transfer war materials to any country whose defence he deemed vital to national security, bypassing a strict neutrality law without technically entering the conflict. The first shipments moved within weeks, directed at an island nation running critically short of everything.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 1941 — FDR signed H.R. 1776 (the bill number was a deliberate wink). By the end of the programme, the US had shipped $50 billion in supplies — equivalent to roughly $800 billion today — to 38 countries. The Soviet Union received about 17 million tons of equipment, including 400,000 jeeps and trucks.

events.title: V-2 Rocket's First Successful Test
events.blurb: A 14-metre liquid-fuelled rocket rose from a Baltic coast test site, climbed above the atmosphere, and travelled 190 kilometres before splashing down — the first object built by human hands to reach space, demonstrating a weapon that could strike cities at supersonic speed with no interception possible by any existing technology.
events.revealBlurb: October 3, 1942, Peenemünde. General Walter Dornberger declared: "This third day of October is the first day of a new era, that of space travel." The same technology later launched the first satellites and moon rockets. The V-2's wartime manufacture killed more people in slave-labour production than it killed as a weapon.

events.title: Second Battle of El Alamein
events.blurb: A British commander who had spent three months rebuilding his army launched a night artillery barrage from 1,000 guns and began grinding through minefields and fortified positions across the Egyptian desert, slowly destroying an Axis force that had driven to within 100 kilometres of a strategically critical port city.
events.revealBlurb: October 23 – November 4, 1942. Montgomery's artillery fired 529,000 shells in the opening barrage. Rommel was on sick leave in Austria when the battle opened; Hitler ordered him back by telegram. After twelve days, Rommel began a 2,000-kilometre retreat across North Africa that ended with final Axis surrender in Tunisia six months later.

events.title: Rosie the Riveter Campaign
events.blurb: A deliberate government and industry campaign to recruit women into heavy industrial and weapons manufacturing work portrayed a bandana-wearing figure flexing her arm above the slogan "We Can Do It!" alongside magazine illustrations that reached millions of households, reshaping public expectations of gender and labour across a nation at industrial-scale mobilisation.
events.revealBlurb: 1942–1943. The number of women in the US workforce rose from 12 million to 20 million — a 57% increase — by 1944. Women built B-29s, welded Liberty ships, and operated cranes. The Westinghouse "We Can Do It!" poster was seen by almost no one during the war; it was rediscovered in the 1980s and became an icon of the feminist movement.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Nintendo Famicom Launches in Japan
events.blurb: A cheap red-and-white 8-bit console hit Japanese shelves the same day as a competing machine. Within a year it had outsold every rival combined, driven fourteen manufacturers out of the market entirely, and established Nintendo as the unchallenged ruler of the Japanese gaming business.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1983 — Nintendo's Family Computer launched in Japan at ¥14,800, head-to-head with Sega's SG-1000. The NES version launched in New York in October 1985. The NES/Famicom line sold 61.91 million units worldwide.

events.title: Super Mario Bros. Released in Japan
events.blurb: A moustachioed Italian plumber leaping over mushrooms and sliding down pipes became the defining character of interactive entertainment. The game shipped as a pack-in with the Nintendo Entertainment System and single-handedly revived an industry that had collapsed two years earlier under the weight of its own shovelware.
events.revealBlurb: September 13, 1985 — Super Mario Bros. launched for Nintendo's Famicom in Japan. It sold over 40 million copies, a record that stood until Wii Sports in 2009. Designer Shigeru Miyamoto built the entire world around the mechanic of a running jump.

events.title: Counter-Strike Released as Standalone
events.blurb: Two amateur developers built a modification for Half-Life in which terrorists and counter-terrorists fought in small tactical maps. Valve noticed the mod's download numbers, purchased the rights, and released it as a standalone product. It became the most-played online game in the world for over a decade, the game credited with institutionalising competitive PC gaming.
events.revealBlurb: November 9, 2000 — Counter-Strike version 1.0 released as a free Half-Life modification. Creators Minh "Gooseman" Le and Jess Cliffe had started the mod in June 1999. In 2023, CS:GO/CS2 peaked at over 1.8 million concurrent Steam players.

events.title: League of Legends Launches
events.blurb: A free-to-play adaptation of a Warcraft III fan modification launched quietly and grew into the most-played PC game on Earth. At its peak over 100 million accounts had been registered, and its annual World Championship filled football stadiums and drew broadcast audiences that dwarfed traditional sporting events. It invented a new genre name — MOBA — and made esports a career path.
events.revealBlurb: October 27, 2009 — Riot Games released League of Legends in North America. It was free-to-play from day one, monetised through cosmetic skins. The 2019 World Championship Finals drew over 100 million unique viewers. Riot was acquired by Tencent in 2011.

events.title: Red Dead Redemption 2 Released
events.blurb: A cowboy open-world game with a 60-hour main story, simulated beard growth, morality consequences for every interaction, and a horse whose bond with the player affected its responsiveness opened the largest weekend in entertainment history. It earned $725 million in three days.
events.revealBlurb: October 26, 2018 — Red Dead Redemption 2 launched for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One. It shipped 17 million copies in its first thirteen days. The game has now sold over 79 million copies. Development reportedly involved teams working 100-hour weeks across five years.

events.title: First Crusade Takes Jerusalem
events.blurb: After a month-long siege and a three-year, 3,000-kilometre march from Europe, an army of Frankish knights and footsoldiers breached the walls of a holy city in the Levant and slaughtered its Muslim and Jewish inhabitants indiscriminately over two days — perhaps 30,000 people. The first crusader state was established with a European dynasty on the throne; it would last 88 years.
events.revealBlurb: July 15, 1099 — the siege was broken when two Flemish knights scaled a siege tower onto the wall. The leaders competed to be the first to reach the Holy Sepulchre. Godfrey of Bouillon refused the crown of a city "where his savior had worn a crown of thorns" — he was titled "Defender" instead.

events.title: Saladin Retakes Jerusalem
events.blurb: A Kurdish Muslim sultan, having crushed a Crusader field army three months earlier at the Horns of Hattin, accepted the peaceful surrender of the holy city from its desperate defenders after an eight-day siege. In contrast to the bloody Frankish sack of the city 88 years earlier, he permitted ransomed Christians to leave with their possessions and freed many who could not pay. News of the fall triggered the Third Crusade.
events.revealBlurb: October 2, 1187 — Saladin. His reputation for chivalry, magnified by his later adversary Richard the Lionheart, made him a hero of medieval European literature despite being its opponent. Dante placed him in Limbo rather than Hell.

events.title: Magna Carta Sealed
events.blurb: Facing armed revolt by his barons after a series of disastrous foreign wars and arbitrary taxation, an English king met them in a meadow beside the Thames and affixed his seal to a 63-clause charter limiting royal power, guaranteeing trial by peers, and making free men subject only to "the law of the land." He repudiated it within ten weeks; civil war resumed.
events.revealBlurb: June 15, 1215 — King John at Runnymede. Only three original copies survive. Clauses against arbitrary imprisonment echo today through American due-process law. The barons were self-interested, not democratic, but the language was universal enough to outlive them.

events.title: Battle of Bannockburn
events.blurb: A smaller Scottish army, dug in with wooden stakes around marshy ground near a castle in central Scotland, destroyed an invading English force three times its size over two days. The English king fled the field. The victory essentially secured Scottish independence, which would be formally recognized 14 years later at the Treaty of Northampton.
events.revealBlurb: June 23-24, 1314 — Robert the Bruce defeats Edward II. The Bruce allegedly split an English knight's skull with an axe in single combat before the main battle. Scotland's national flag flew over Stirling Castle the next morning.

events.title: Battle of Agincourt
events.blurb: An exhausted English army, heavily outnumbered, caught in thick mud on a narrow front between two woods in northern France, stood behind sharpened wooden stakes and cut down the armored flower of French nobility with longbows at point-blank range. The French dead included a constable, three dukes, and over 1,500 knights; English losses were perhaps 400. Shakespeare would turn it into a speech 180 years later.
events.revealBlurb: October 25, 1415 — Henry V on St. Crispin's Day. Henry ordered the slaughter of prisoners mid-battle when he feared a rear attack; this remains controversial. The longbow's armor-piercing arrowheads were called "bodkins."

events.title: Pac-Man Reaches North America
events.blurb: A Japanese arcade cabinet featuring a yellow circular character navigating a maze while consuming dots and evading four coloured ghosts began distribution across North American arcades. Within 18 months it had been installed in over 100,000 locations and grossed more revenue than all theatrical box office receipts in America that year combined.

events.title: Tylenol Murders
events.blurb: Seven people in the Chicago area died after taking over-the-counter acetaminophen capsules that had been laced with potassium cyanide by an unknown tamperer. The crisis triggered a nationwide recall of 31 million bottles, launched the tamper-resistant packaging industry, and reshaped pharmaceutical manufacturing standards permanently. Johnson & Johnson's swift and transparent response became a classic case study in crisis management. The killer was never identified.
events.revealBlurb: September 29-October 1, 1982 — seven deaths in Chicago suburbs. Pills had been purchased, tampered with, and returned to drugstore shelves. James William Lewis, a former suspect, died in 2023 maintaining his innocence. Tamper-proof packaging became a federal mandate within six months.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Spice Girls' "Wannabe"
events.blurb: A British pop group of five young women released their debut single — a bouncy three-minute track with a rap-like opening, shot on a single take in a Lisbon hotel — hit number one in 37 countries over the following months. The five — styled "Scary," "Sporty," "Baby," "Ginger," and "Posh" — would dominate late-1990s pop culture with a "Girl Power" message that was earnest, commercial, and enormously successful. They sold 100 million records globally.
events.revealBlurb: July 8, 1996 — Spice Girls: Melanie B (Scary), Melanie C (Sporty), Emma Bunton (Baby), Geri Halliwell (Ginger), Victoria Adams (Posh). The video was shot in a single day at the Hotel Palácio in Portugal. Victoria Beckham married David Beckham in 1999; she launched a fashion career later.

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: First ARPANET Message
events.blurb: A graduate student at a California university tried to log in remotely to a computer at a research institute 560 kilometres north. He typed "L," then "O," then tried to type "G" — and the receiving computer crashed. The first ever message transmitted between two computers on what would grow into the global network was thus the two-letter sequence "lo."
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1969 — UCLA to the Stanford Research Institute. The student was Charley Kline. ARPANET was funded by the Pentagon to enable communication after a nuclear strike. The network went from 4 nodes to 37 in three years.

events.title: eBay Founded
events.blurb: A 28-year-old Iranian-American software engineer set up an online auction site over the Labor Day weekend, initially as a hobby project on a personal server. One of the first items sold was a broken laser pointer for $14.83. When he emailed the buyer to check whether he understood it was broken, the buyer replied that he collected broken laser pointers. The founder realized he had a business on his hands.
events.revealBlurb: September 3, 1995 — Pierre Omidyar. He originally named it AuctionWeb; renamed eBay in 1997, short for Echo Bay Technology, his consulting firm. The first commission was sent as a personal check for $241.19.

events.title: YouTube Launched
events.blurb: Three former PayPal employees, reportedly frustrated that they couldn't easily share a video of a dinner party or (by an alternate legend) a wardrobe malfunction from a recent sporting event, registered a domain name for a video-sharing site. The site's first uploaded video, "Me at the zoo," was an 18-second clip of one of the founders standing in front of elephants at the San Diego Zoo. Google bought them for $1.65 billion in stock twenty months later.
events.revealBlurb: February 14, 2005 — Chad Hurley, Steve Chen, Jawed Karim. The "Me at the zoo" video is still online, with over 350 million views. Users now upload over 500 hours of video every minute.

events.title: Bitcoin Whitepaper Published
events.blurb: A nine-page academic paper titled "Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System," written under a pseudonym, was posted to a cryptography mailing list in the middle of the global financial crisis. It described a digital currency that didn't need banks or central authorities to verify transactions. The first block of the currency was mined two months later; the identity of its author has never been established.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 2008 — "Satoshi Nakamoto." The genesis block, mined January 3, 2009, contained the text "Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks" from that day's Times. Suspected Satoshis have included Hal Finney, Nick Szabo, Craig Wright (contested), and Dorian Nakamoto (denied).

events.title: Cambridge Analytica Scandal
events.blurb: A former employee of a small British political consultancy went public with allegations that the firm had harvested personal data from some 87 million Facebook users, mostly without their knowledge or consent, and used it to build psychographic voter-targeting models for the 2016 U.S. presidential and UK Brexit campaigns. Facebook's stock lost $100 billion in market value in ten days. Its CEO was subsequently hauled before the U.S. Congress and the European Parliament.
events.revealBlurb: March 17, 2018 — whistleblower Christopher Wylie in The Observer and New York Times. Cambridge Analytica went bankrupt within two months. Facebook was later fined $5 billion by the U.S. FTC — the largest fine ever for a privacy violation, but about a month's profit for the company.

events.title: Hanging Gardens of Babylon
events.blurb: Tradition holds that a Babylonian king built a tiered rooftop garden at his palace for his wife, homesick for the mountainous landscape of her native Media. The structure — described by Greek writers as having stone terraces planted with trees and shrubs irrigated by an elaborate water-lifting machine — was counted among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. No archaeological evidence of them has ever been identified at Babylon, leading some scholars to believe they existed instead at Nineveh under a different king.
events.revealBlurb: c. 600 BCE — traditionally attributed to Nebuchadnezzar II. A leading alternative theory attributes them to Sennacherib at Nineveh, a century earlier. Of the Seven Wonders, only the Pyramids survive and the Hanging Gardens are the one whose very existence is still in question.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Statue of Liberty Dedicated
events.blurb: A 46-metre-tall copper statue of a robed woman holding a torch, a gift from the French people commemorating American independence (with an eye toward French republican aspirations), was dedicated on a small island in New York Harbor in the rain. It had been designed by a French sculptor, its internal iron framework engineered by the man who would five years later design a certain Paris tower, and shipped across the Atlantic in 350 pieces.
events.revealBlurb: October 28, 1886 — sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi; engineer Gustave Eiffel. The statue was meant to arrive for the 1876 centennial; it missed by a decade due to fundraising troubles. The poem on its pedestal ("Give me your tired, your poor...") was added in 1903 from a sonnet by Emma Lazarus.

events.title: Fallingwater Completed
events.blurb: A 70-year-old American architect completed a weekend house for a Pittsburgh department-store owner, cantilevered dramatically over a waterfall in rural western Pennsylvania. The design — with horizontal reinforced-concrete terraces seemingly floating over the rock and water — reimagined what residential architecture could be and became a singular icon of 20th-century organic architecture. The cantilevered decks began sagging within years; an expensive 21st-century restoration saved the house.
events.revealBlurb: 1937 — Frank Lloyd Wright for the Kaufmann family in Bear Run, PA. The Kaufmanns had expected the house to sit across from the waterfall looking at it; Wright insisted on placing it over the water. Wright won the Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1941 and the AIA Gold Medal in 1949.

events.title: Battle of New Orleans
events.blurb: General Andrew Jackson's patchwork army of Tennessee frontiersmen, Louisiana militia, free Black soldiers, Choctaw warriors, and pirates under Jean Lafitte decisively routed an 8,000-strong British force attempting to seize New Orleans, killing or wounding roughly 2,000 redcoats while suffering fewer than 70 American casualties. The lopsided victory made Jackson a national hero and propelled him to the presidency.
events.revealBlurb: January 8, 1815 — Chalmette, Louisiana. The Treaty of Ghent ending the War of 1812 had been signed 15 days earlier — news hadn't arrived. The battle had zero effect on the war's official outcome but enormous effect on American mythology and Jackson's political career.

events.title: Wall Street Crash: Black Tuesday
events.blurb: On the 29th of that month, stock markets collapsed in a cascade of panic selling that wiped out an estimated $14 billion in a single day, erasing the paper fortunes of thousands of investors and devastating the banking system. The crash followed years of rampant speculation fueled by easy credit and margin buying, in which millions of Americans had purchased stocks with borrowed money against collateral that suddenly no longer existed.
events.revealBlurb: October 29, 1929 — New York Stock Exchange. More than 16 million shares traded on Black Tuesday — a record that stood for decades. The Dow lost nearly 50% of its value by mid-November. Economists still debate whether the crash caused the Great Depression or merely triggered an underlying structural collapse.

events.title: Brown v. Board of Education Ruling
events.blurb: A unanimous Supreme Court held that racially segregated public schools were inherently unequal and violated the Fourteenth Amendment's Equal Protection Clause, overturning the 1896 Plessy v. Ferguson doctrine of "separate but equal." The unanimous 9–0 decision, written by Chief Justice Earl Warren after months of behind-the-scenes persuasion, applied to all public schools and laid the legal foundation for desegregation across American society.
events.revealBlurb: May 17, 1954 — Washington, D.C. Chief Justice Warren had been appointed by Eisenhower, who privately thought the ruling a mistake. The lead attorney for the plaintiffs was Thurgood Marshall — who would later become the first Black justice on the very court he argued before.

events.title: Iran Hostage Crisis Begins
events.blurb: Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and seized 52 American diplomats and staff as hostages, demanding that the United States extradite the deposed Shah — who was receiving cancer treatment in New York — and return his assets. The hostages were held for 444 days, paralyzing the Carter presidency and reshaping American politics for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1979 — Tehran, Iran. The hostages were released on January 20, 1981 — literally within minutes of Ronald Reagan being inaugurated. Carter spent his last night as president awake, monitoring the negotiations.

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Mark Spitz Wins Seventh Munich Gold
events.blurb: An American swimmer won his seventh gold medal of the Munich Games by anchoring the 4×100-metre medley relay team, setting a world record in every individual event he entered. No athlete had ever won more gold medals at a single Olympic Games, and he set or broke a world record in each of his seven finals.

events.title: The Rumble in the Jungle
events.blurb: A 32-year-old heavyweight boxing challenger, widely predicted to lose to the younger and vastly more powerful champion, leaned back against the ropes for seven rounds and absorbed punishing body blows — a tactic he later nicknamed "rope-a-dope." In the 8th, when the champion visibly tired, the challenger delivered a flurry of punches that knocked him out. The fight was held in an African capital as part of a pioneering pan-African promotion.
events.revealBlurb: October 30, 1974 — Muhammad Ali KO'd George Foreman at the Stade du 20 Mai in Kinshasa, Zaire (now Democratic Republic of the Congo). Promoter Don King organized it. The event was immortalized in the 1996 documentary "When We Were Kings."

events.title: Cubs Win World Series
events.blurb: The Chicago Cubs won their first World Series championship in 108 years, defeating the Cleveland Indians in a 10-inning seventh game interrupted by a rain delay. The Cubs' championship drought — dating back to 1908 — was the longest in American professional sports. Their 1945 loss had been attributed by fans to the "Curse of the Billy Goat," thrown at the owner of a neighbourhood tavern who had been asked to remove his pet goat from a World Series game.
events.revealBlurb: November 2-3, 2016 — Cubs 8, Indians 7 in 10 innings at Progressive Field, Cleveland. The game ended at 12:47 AM local time on November 3. Cubs manager Joe Maddon, third baseman Kris Bryant, and first baseman Anthony Rizzo led the championship team. Chicago celebrated with a victory parade of 5 million people.

events.title: Messi Wins World Cup
events.blurb: A 35-year-old Argentine forward, in his fifth and final World Cup tournament, led his team to a 3-3 draw against France in the final, then won a penalty shootout 4-2 at a Qatari stadium. He scored two of the final's goals himself, then converted his penalty. The tournament's signature absence from his glittering career — the World Cup — was at last his. It was widely described as the greatest World Cup final ever played.
events.revealBlurb: December 18, 2022 — Argentina 3-3 France (4-2 pens), Lusail Stadium, Qatar. Messi and Kylian Mbappé combined for six goals between them. Messi had already won seven Ballon d'Or awards, a record; he would win an eighth in 2023. Mbappé became the first to score a hat-trick in a World Cup final since Geoff Hurst in 1966.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Luther Posts the 95 Theses
events.blurb: A 33-year-old German university theologian sent his local archbishop a letter enclosing a 95-point list of academic propositions challenging the papal indulgence system — the practice of selling forgiveness of sins. By tradition, he also posted the Latin theses on the door of his university church, which served as a community bulletin board. Copies reached print within weeks and spread across Germany. He had intended academic debate; he ignited the Protestant Reformation.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1517 — Martin Luther at Wittenberg Castle Church. Most scholars doubt the physical nailing-to-the-door story; the letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Mainz is well-documented. October 31 is now celebrated as Reformation Day in many Protestant countries.

events.title: Fall of Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: After a three-month siege — during which Spanish-allied Indigenous forces demolished the city district by district, channeled the causeways, and introduced a devastating smallpox epidemic — the last Aztec emperor surrendered in a canoe on the lake as his capital burned. The Spaniards, led by Cortés, renamed the ruins and built a viceregal capital on them. The Aztec empire ceased to exist; the Spanish conquest of the Americas was underway.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1521 — Cuauhtémoc surrendered to Cortés. The city's population had dropped from perhaps 200,000 to under 50,000 through disease, siege starvation, and fighting. The Spanish built Mexico City on the drained lakebed — which continues to sink today at 50 cm per year.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: Elizabeth I Accession
events.blurb: A 25-year-old unmarried princess, the daughter of a beheaded second queen who had once been declared a bastard, became Queen of England on the death of her half-sister. She had survived imprisonment and political marginalization under her sister's Catholic restoration. Her 44-year reign would see the English settlement of Ireland, the defeat of the Spanish Armada, the flowering of Shakespeare, and the establishment of a Protestant national church still in existence.
events.revealBlurb: November 17, 1558 — Elizabeth I Tudor succeeds Mary I. She reportedly received the news sitting under an oak tree at Hatfield House. She never married, styled herself the "Virgin Queen," and died at 69. The state of Virginia — briefly colonized under her — is named for her.
